questions.q: Affinity of a drug refers to its:
opts: Tendency to bind to the target
Maximum effect produced at the target
Relative dose required for a given effect
Duration of action at the receptor
questions.exp: In the flowchart, 'drug binds to target' corresponds to tendency to bind = affinity. (Book p18)

questions.q: Efficacy of a drug is defined as the:
opts: Tendency of the drug to bind its target
Relative dose needed to produce an effect
Safety of the drug in a population
questions.exp: The flowchart links 'produces effect' to the maximum effect produced, i.e. efficacy - which the book marks as clinically most important. (Book p18)

questions.q: Of affinity, efficacy and potency, which is described as clinically most important?
questions.exp: The page marks efficacy with the note 'clinically most important', because it decides the maximum benefit a drug can give. (Book p18)

questions.q: Potency of a drug refers to the:
opts: Relative dose of a drug required to produce a particular effect
Maximum effect the drug can produce
Tendency to bind to its receptor
questions.exp: Potency = relative dose of a drug required to produce a particular effect. (Book p18)

questions.q: A drug that produces the same effect at a LOWER dose is said to have:
questions.exp: The lesser the dose needed to bring about the effect, the greater the potency - potency and dose requirement are inversely related. (Book p18)

questions.q: Which statement about potency and efficacy is correct?
opts: Potency is a matter of dose, efficacy is a matter of the maximum response attainable
Potency is the maximum response and efficacy is the dose required
Both describe the same property of a drug
Both are independent of dose and response
questions.exp: Potency concerns the dose needed for a given effect, while efficacy is the maximum effect produced - two separate properties. (Book p18)

questions.q: A quantal dose response curve records a response which is:
questions.exp: Quantal DRC: response is binary (present/absent), e.g. sedatives and fertility drugs, and is studied in a population. (Book p18)

questions.q: Which drugs are given as examples for a quantal response?
opts: Drugs modifying blood pressure and heart rate
questions.exp: The examples given under quantal DRC are sedatives and fertility drugs, where the effect either occurs or does not. (Book p18)

questions.q: The quantal dose response curve is studied in:
questions.exp: The quantal DRC is studied in a population, in contrast to the graded DRC which is studied in an individual. (Book p18)

questions.q: ED50 is the dose at which 50% of the population experiences:
questions.exp: ED50 is the dose at which 50% of the population experiences therapeutic effects. (Book p18)

questions.q: TD50 is the dose at which 50% of the population experiences:
questions.exp: TD50 is the dose at which 50% of the population experiences toxic effects. (Book p18)

questions.q: LD50 is the dose at which 50% experience:
questions.exp: LD50 is the dose at which 50% of animals experience lethal effects. (Book p18)

questions.q: In the quantal DRC table, ED50 is used as a marker of:
questions.exp: The table marks ED50 as the marker of potency; TD50 and LD50 are markers of toxicity. (Book p18)

questions.q: Which parameters are used as markers of toxicity in the quantal DRC?
opts: LD50 only, since TD50 is not used
questions.exp: The marker column shows potency opposite ED50 and toxicity opposite both TD50 and LD50. (Book p18)

questions.q: On the quantal dose response graph, response in % of population is plotted against:
questions.exp: The graph plots response in % population on the y-axis against log dose on the x-axis, with therapeutic, toxic and lethal curves and the ED50, TD50 and LD50 marked at the 50% line. (Book p18)

questions.q: On the quantal graph, the curve lying to the LEFT is that of:
questions.exp: The therapeutic effects curve is leftmost since lower doses produce benefit, with toxicity and then lethal effects appearing further to the right. (Book p18)

questions.q: The lethal effects curve on the quantal graph is:
opts: Furthest to the right, because animals die only at the highest doses
Leftmost, because death occurs at low doses
Absent, because lethality is not studied
questions.exp: With log dose on the x-axis, lethal effects (in animals) appear furthest right, after the toxic effects curve. (Book p18)

questions.q: Therapeutic index (TI) is a measurement of:
questions.exp: The page describes TI as measurement of the safety of a drug. (Book p18)

questions.q: In HUMANS the therapeutic index is calculated as:
questions.exp: The book gives humans: TD50/ED50 and animals: LD50/ED50 for the therapeutic index. (Book p18)

questions.q: In ANIMALS the therapeutic index is calculated as:
questions.exp: For animals the therapeutic index is LD50/ED50, whereas in humans it is TD50/ED50. (Book p18)

questions.q: A drug with a LOW therapeutic index:
opts: Is safe only in a narrow dosage range and has an increased chance of toxicity
Is safe over a wide dosage range
Has high efficacy but low potency
Cannot produce toxicity at any dose
questions.exp: Low TI means the drug is safe only in a narrow dosage range, with an increased chance of toxicity - lithium is the example given. (Book p18)

questions.q: A drug with a HIGH therapeutic index is:
opts: Safe in a wide dosage range
Safe only in a narrow dosage range
questions.exp: High TI means the drug is safe in a wide dosage range; low TI (lithium) means safety only in a narrow range. (Book p18)

questions.q: Which drug is quoted as the example of a low therapeutic index?
questions.exp: Lithium is the example given for a low TI, which is why its plasma levels must be monitored. (Book p18)

questions.q: In the lithium concentration-time curve, the therapeutic window lies between:
questions.exp: The figure marks lithium's therapeutic window from 0.6 meq/L (minimum effective concentration) up to 1.5 meq/L (minimum toxic concentration). (Book p18)

questions.q: The lower boundary of the therapeutic window is the:
questions.exp: The lower dashed line is the minimum effective concentration - below it there is no effect. (Book p18)

questions.q: The upper boundary of the therapeutic window is the:
questions.exp: The upper dashed line is the minimum toxic concentration; above it, toxicity occurs. (Book p18)

questions.q: In the therapeutic window figure, the zone below the minimum effective concentration of lithium is labelled:
questions.exp: The grey zone below 0.6 meq/L is labelled 'no effect', the green zone is the therapeutic window and the red zone above 1.5 meq/L is toxicity. (Book p18)

questions.q: What is the plasma concentration range of lithium that is toxic?
questions.exp: Plasma lithium above the minimum toxic concentration of 1.5 meq/L lies in the toxicity band of the figure. (Book p18)

questions.q: The therapeutic window is best defined as the:
opts: Range of plasma concentration between the minimum effective and minimum toxic concentrations
Dose at which 50% of a population responds
Range of doses with no effect
questions.exp: The figure shows the therapeutic window as the band of plasma concentration between the minimum effective concentration and the minimum toxic concentration. (Book p18)

questions.q: A graded (quantified) response is seen with drugs modifying:
opts: Blood pressure, heart rate and blood glucose levels
questions.exp: Graded response = quantified response, e.g. drugs modifying BP, HR and blood glucose levels, and it is studied in an individual. (Book p19)

questions.q: The graded dose response curve is studied in:
questions.exp: The graded DRC is studied in an individual, whereas the quantal DRC is studied in a population. (Book p19)

questions.q: On the graded DRC, the response is plotted on the y-axis and ______ on the x-axis.
questions.exp: The graded DRC graph plots response (0-100) against log dose, with the three sigmoid curves of drugs A, B and C. (Book p19)

questions.q: In the graded DRC table, efficacy is described as:
opts: Determined by response, the more the height the greater the efficacy
Determined by the dose, the further left the greater the efficacy
More to the right meaning greater potency
questions.exp: Efficacy is read off the height of the curve: more the height, greater the efficacy, giving the comparative order B > A > C. (Book p19)

questions.q: According to the graded DRC table, the comparative order of efficacy is:
questions.exp: The table's comparative column for efficacy reads B > A > C, following the heights of the three curves. (Book p19)

questions.q: In the graded DRC table, potency is determined by:
opts: A lesser dose producing the same effect - the more to the left, the greater the potency
The maximum height of the curve
questions.exp: Potency: lesser dose for the same effect means greater potency, and graphically 'more to the left = higher potency'. (Book p19)

questions.q: The comparative order of potency in the graded DRC table is:
questions.exp: The comparative column for potency reads PA > PB > PC, i.e. drug A is the most potent because its curve lies furthest left. (Book p19)

questions.q: On the graded DRC, drug A is:
opts: The most potent (leftmost) but not the most efficacious
The most efficacious (highest) but not the most potent
Both the most potent and the most efficacious
The least potent and the least efficacious
questions.exp: Drug A lies furthest left (highest potency, PA > PB > PC) while drug B gives the greatest height (highest efficacy, B > A > C). (Book p19)

questions.q: On the graded DRC, drug B has:
questions.exp: Efficacy follows the height of the curve, and B has the greatest height, giving the order B > A > C for efficacy. (Book p19)

questions.q: In the graded DRC table, affinity is described as:
opts: Comparable between drugs of the same mechanism of action
Comparable between drugs of different mechanisms of action
Determined by the height of the curve
Independent of the position of the curve
questions.exp: Affinity is comparable between drugs of the same MOA, and only between parallel lines; more to the left means higher affinity. (Book p19)

questions.q: As per the affinity column, affinity can be compared only between:
questions.exp: The table notes affinity is comparable between drugs of the same MOA - determined graphically 'only comparable between parallel lines'. (Book p19)

questions.q: In the graded DRC table, the comparative order of affinity is:
opts: A > B, because drug C is not parallel
questions.exp: With C not parallel to the others, affinity can only be compared between A and B - the table gives A > B. (Book p19)

questions.q: Drug C in the graded DRC is excluded from the affinity comparison because:
opts: C is not parallel to the other curves
questions.exp: The affinity column states the comparison holds only between parallel lines, and the table records 'A > B (C is not parallel)'. (Book p19)

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes efficacy from potency on a graded DRC?
opts: Efficacy is judged by the height of the curve and potency by its position on the x-axis
Efficacy is judged by the position and potency by the height
Both are judged by the height of the curve
Both are judged by the slope of the curve
questions.exp: Height of the curve gives efficacy, while position along the log dose axis gives potency - the further left, the more potent. (Book p19)

questions.q: The effect of a full agonist upon binding to its receptor is:
opts: Opposite to the nature of the receptor
questions.exp: The drug receptor interaction table gives full agonists a maximum effect (curve A). (Book p19)

questions.q: The effect of a partial agonist upon binding to its receptor is:
questions.exp: Partial agonists produce a submaximal effect (curve B), less than a full agonist whatever the dose. (Book p19)

questions.q: An antagonist, upon binding to its receptor, produces:
opts: An effect opposite to the receptor's nature
questions.exp: Antagonists have no effect of their own upon binding (curve C) - their action is seen only in the presence of an agonist. (Book p19)

questions.q: An inverse agonist, upon binding to its receptor, produces:
opts: An effect opposite to the nature of the receptor
questions.exp: The inverse agonist produces an effect opposite to the nature of the receptors (curve D), falling below the baseline of no effect. (Book p19)

questions.q: In terms of net effect in the body when endogenous full agonists are present, a partial agonist produces:
questions.exp: With endogenous full agonists present, partial agonists give mild antagonism, antagonists moderate antagonism and inverse agonists severe antagonism. (Book p19)

questions.q: Which agent produces moderate antagonism of endogenous full agonists?
questions.exp: The table's net effect row reads: partial agonist - mild antagonism, antagonist - moderate antagonism, inverse agonist - severe antagonism. (Book p19)

questions.q: Which agent produces severe antagonism of endogenous full agonists?
questions.exp: Inverse agonists produce an effect opposite to the receptor's nature, which in the presence of endogenous full agonists amounts to severe antagonism. (Book p19)

questions.q: Intrinsic efficacy, the mathematical representation of efficacy, for a FULL agonist is:
questions.exp: The table assigns intrinsic efficacy +1 to full agonists, between 1 and 0 to partial agonists, 0 to antagonists and -1 to inverse agonists. (Book p19)

questions.q: The intrinsic efficacy of a partial agonist lies:
questions.exp: Partial agonists have an intrinsic efficacy between 1 and 0 - more than an antagonist but less than a full agonist. (Book p19)

questions.q: The intrinsic efficacy of an antagonist is:
questions.exp: Antagonists have an intrinsic efficacy of 0, which corresponds to producing no effect upon binding. (Book p19)

questions.q: The intrinsic efficacy of an inverse agonist is:
questions.exp: Inverse agonists are given an intrinsic efficacy of -1, matching their effect opposite to the nature of the receptor. (Book p19)

questions.q: On the dose-response figure of drug receptor interactions, the curve that dips below the baseline of no effect represents:
questions.exp: Curve A is maximal (full agonist), B submaximal (partial agonist), C flat at no effect (antagonist) and D falls to the opposite effect (inverse agonist). (Book p19)

questions.q: On the drug receptor interaction graph, the flat line at the level of no effect represents:
questions.exp: Curve C stays at 'no effect' across the dose range - the antagonist, which produces no action of its own. (Book p19)

questions.q: According to the note on this page, the type of drug most commonly used among these is:
questions.exp: The note box states that antagonists are the m/c used, even though they produce no effect of their own. (Book p19)

questions.q: Which pair of agents and intrinsic efficacy is correctly matched?
questions.exp: Correct values are +1 for full agonists, between 1 and 0 for partial agonists, 0 for antagonists and -1 for inverse agonists. (Book p19)

questions.q: A patient on a full agonist for asthma is given a partial agonist at the same receptor. Which effect is expected?
opts: Mild antagonism, because the partial agonist produces only a submaximal effect
Severe antagonism with complete loss of effect
No change, because both are agonists
An effect opposite to the receptor's nature
questions.exp: With an endogenous full agonist present, a partial agonist produces only a submaximal effect and therefore mild antagonism. (Book p19)

questions.q: Comparing curves, which statement about a full versus a partial agonist is correct?
opts: A full agonist reaches a maximal effect while a partial agonist plateaus at a submaximal effect
A partial agonist reaches a maximal effect while a full agonist is submaximal
Both reach the same maximal effect at different doses
Neither can be compared on a graded dose response curve
questions.exp: In the figure, A (full agonist) rises to maximal, B (partial agonist) plateaus at submaximal, C (antagonist) stays at no effect and D (inverse agonist) moves to the opposite effect. (Book p19)

units.title: Affinity, Efficacy and Potency
units.guide: A drug's tendency to bind its target is affinity; the maximum effect it produces is efficacy, and efficacy is the clinically most important property because it fixes the ceiling of benefit. Potency is a different matter - the relative dose needed for a given effect, so the lesser the dose, the greater the potency. A graded (quantified) response, such as a change in BP, HR or blood glucose, is studied in an individual.

units.title: Quantal DRC: ED50, TD50 and LD50
units.guide: The quantal DRC records a binary, all-or-none response (sedation, fertility) in a population, plotting the percentage of responders against log dose. ED50 is the dose at which half the population gets a therapeutic effect and marks potency, while TD50 (toxic) and LD50 (lethal, in animals) mark toxicity; on the graph the therapeutic curve sits leftmost and the lethal curve furthest right.

units.title: Therapeutic Index and Therapeutic Window
units.guide: The therapeutic index measures safety: TD50/ED50 in humans and LD50/ED50 in animals. A low index, as with lithium, means safety only within a narrow dosage range and a high chance of toxicity, whereas a high index allows a wide range. The therapeutic window is the corridor between the minimum effective concentration (0.6 meq/L for lithium) and the minimum toxic concentration (1.5 meq/L) - below it there is no effect and above it toxicity.

units.title: Graded DRC: Height, Position and Parallel Lines
units.guide: On the graded DRC (response versus log dose in an individual) efficacy is read from the height of the curve and potency from its position - more to the left means more potent. In the figure, efficacy runs B > A > C and potency PA > PB > PC, so drug A is the most potent yet B the most efficacious. Affinity is comparable only between drugs of the same MOA and only between parallel lines, which is why C is excluded and the order is A > B.

units.title: Full, Partial, Antagonist, Inverse: The Table
units.guide: The interaction table grades four behaviours: a full agonist gives a maximum effect (+1 intrinsic efficacy), a partial agonist a submaximal effect (between 1 and 0), an antagonist no effect (0) and an inverse agonist an effect opposite to the receptor's nature (-1). Against endogenous full agonists these translate into mild, moderate and severe antagonism respectively. On the figure, A rises to maximal, B plateaus submaximally, C stays flat and D dips below the no-effect line.

units.title: Clinical Reading of Agonists and Antagonists
units.guide: The single most useful clinical fact from this table is its footnote: antagonists are the most commonly used drugs, even though they exert no effect of their own. Adding a partial agonist to a patient already on a full agonist yields only mild antagonism, because a partial agonist can never match a full agonist's maximal response.
